text: Bots start guessing SSH passwords on internet facing servers within minutes of them coming online.

text: And when teams harden servers by hand from a checklist, every server ends up a little different, and nobody notices when someone quietly switches password login back on.

text: One design detail: the role reads the running values first, and writes only the ones that differ. So when this role reports changed, it really means something drifted.
tts: One design detail: the role reads the running values first, and writes only the ones that differ. So when this role reports changed, it really means something drifted.

text: Role three is SSH. Only members of the ssh users group may log in, root may never log in, and the only accepted method is a public key. Password and keyboard interactive logins are off.
tts: Role three is S-S-H. Only members of the S-S-H users group may log in, root may never log in, and the only accepted method is a public key. Password and keyboard interactive logins are off.

text: Tunnels and forwarding are switched off, so a login is a shell, not a network path into the server.
tts: Tunnels and forwarding are switched off, so a login is a shell, not a network path into the server.

text: Only modern key exchange, ciphers and MACs are allowed, weak Diffie Hellman groups are removed, and verbose logging records the key fingerprint of every login.

text: Automation that changes SSH and the firewall can lock you out of every server at once. So this project has four safety nets. First, the guards: the run stops if no admin key exists, if the allowed SSH groups are empty, or if the firewall has no SSH rule.
